sections.section: Royal chapel and the way to the courtyard

tracks.room: Entrada · Puerta del Lagarto or Puerta del Príncipe
tracks.title: Welcome to the Catedral de Sevilla
tracks.where: Just past the entrance check, standing aside out of the flow. At the Puerta del Lagarto, the door by the Giralda into the covered gallery of the Patio de los Naranjos, with a crocodile hanging overhead [O1]. At the Puerta del Príncipe, the door in the south arm of the transept, with Columbus's tomb, four heralds carrying a coffin, nearby [O2, O12].
tracks.what: Orientation: the mosque, the cathedral from 1248, the Gothic church after 1401; UNESCO World Heritage 1987 (Cathedral, Alcázar, Archivo de Indias); how the guide works (one route, three lengths; Extras not on the shorter versions); the Giralda first; working church; one way through; both entrances; non-climbers.
tracks.listen: What this place was before it was a cathedral, how the guide works, and how to get from your door to the Giralda.

tracks.title: Giralda — The minaret of 1184
tracks.where: At the tower door or on the first ramps of the Giralda [O3, O4]: broad, gently sloping ramps with no stairs, turning between the outer wall and the central core. Heard while climbing; keep moving, keep right.
tracks.what: The Giralda, Almohad minaret ordered 1184 under the caliph Abu Ya'qub Yusuf, carried on under al-Mansur; laid out by Ahmad ibn Baso, continued in brick by Ali al-Ghumari; gilded yamur raised March 1198, brought down by the 1356 earthquake; Renaissance belfry of the sixteenth century; close to 100 m to the tip of the weathervane.
tracks.listen: How the minaret was built, the golden balls that crowned it, and how it became a bell tower that the world copied.

tracks.title: Giralda — Thirty-four ramps
tracks.where: On the ramps inside the Giralda, a few turns above the door [O4]: a wide, gently sloping ramp between the outer wall and the central core, people coming down on the other side. Heard while climbing; keep moving, keep right.
tracks.what: The Almohad interior of the Giralda: 34 ramps and 7 vaulted chambers; ramps wide enough for a rider on horseback; double-walled tubular structure; more than 140 reused capitals and bases; builders' sketches found on the four faces during the 2017–2024 restoration.
tracks.listen: Why the tower has ramps instead of stairs, the stones it borrowed, and the builders' sketches restorers have just found.

tracks.title: Giralda — The view from the bells
tracks.where: At the top of the ramps, on the bell level of the Giralda, at an opening on the side that looks down on the Patio de los Naranjos: rows of orange trees in a walled courtyard far below [O5]. Stand back from the openings to let others pass.
tracks.what: The Renaissance belfry of the Giralda by Hernán Ruiz the Younger (contract 17 Dec 1557, after a competition; crowned 13 Aug 1568) on the Almohad minaret; the view of the Patio de los Naranjos and the cathedral roofs; the crossing dome's collapse in 1511; DATED: Phase VI works on the bell chamber and Renaissance crown since April 2026; the lily vase that fell in February 2026.
tracks.listen: Who put a Renaissance crown on a minaret, what you can see of the mosque from up here, and what has happened to the tower this year.

tracks.title: Giralda · Extra · Twenty-four bells
tracks.where: Still on the bell level of the Giralda, in the Renaissance bell chamber at the top of the ramps [O5]. Stand back from the openings and out of the way of the ramps.
tracks.what: The Giralda's 24 bells; the largest, Santa María la Mayor, "la Gorda", cast 1588 by Juan de Balabarca, about 5,362 kg; Bartolomé Morel had a hand in casting seven of the bells; DATED: Phase VI rebuilding six bell frames with damping and replacing the bell's 2021 emergency shoring.
tracks.listen: The biggest bell in the tower, her nickname, and the works that are giving her a new support.

tracks.title: Giralda — From mosque to cathedral
tracks.where: On the ramps of the Giralda, going down, keeping to the right [O6]. Heard while walking; no need to stop.
tracks.what: The Great Mosque of Seville, ordered 1172 by the Almohad caliph Abu Ya'qub Yusuf, prayer hall 1172–76, minaret finished 1198 under his son; 1248 Fernando III takes Seville and the mosque becomes the cathedral; 1401 the chapter's decision; the "think us mad" tradition and the more sober wording handed down; building from the 1430s; finished 1506, opened 11 May 1507; what the mosque left: the minaret, the courtyard and the Puerta del Perdón.
tracks.listen: How a mosque became a cathedral, the famous "mad" quotation and what the decision says, as it has come down to us, and what survives of the mosque.

tracks.room: Catedral · at the foot of the Giralda
tracks.title: The nave — A hollow mountain
tracks.where: Inside the church, just out of the way of the Giralda door, at the corner of the building where the tower stands [O7]. Rows of massive pillars run away from you; the great enclosures of the choir and the main chapel fill the middle of the church.
tracks.what: The Gothic cathedral as a whole: "hollow mountain"; five naves, "the largest Gothic building in Europe" (UNESCO and the Cathedral); Guinness, the cathedral covering the greatest area (126.2 × 82.6 m); plan on the footprint of the mosque; orientation: Capilla Mayor and Coro in the central nave, Capilla Real at the head, the sacristies and chapter house.
tracks.listen: How big this church really is, why it is so wide, and how it is laid out, so the rest of the visit makes sense.

tracks.title: Capilla Mayor — The Retablo Mayor
tracks.where: At the crossing, the middle of the church where the transept crosses the nave, facing the Capilla Mayor's iron grille [O8]. Behind it rises a wall of gilded and painted wooden scenes, nearly thirty metres high, with a crucifix at the very top. The choir is behind you.
tracks.what: Retablo Mayor of the Capilla Mayor, begun 1482 under Pieter Dancart; first phase to 1529 (a second Flemish master 1497–1505, Pedro Millán, Jorge Fernández and his brother Alejo); side sections 1550–1564 (Roque Balduque, Juan Bautista Vázquez, Pedro de Heredia); polychrome and gilded wood, nearly 30 m high, almost 20 m wide; 44 reliefs, more than 200 saint figures, 8 reliefs of the Kings of Israel and Judah; 14th-century Gothic Calvary with the "Christ of the Million"; restoration completed 2014.
tracks.listen: Who made the great altarpiece over eighty-two years, how big it really is, and the crucifix at the top.

tracks.title: Capilla Mayor · Extra · The iron grilles
tracks.where: Still at the crossing, facing the Capilla Mayor: the tall iron grilles, the rejas, that close off the main chapel and through which you see the altarpiece [O8].
tracks.what: The rejas (iron grilles) of the Capilla Mayor, early sixteenth century, largely by the Dominican friar Francisco de Salamanca and other Seville ironworkers; Salamanca summoned to Seville in 1518; the high-altar pulpits, 1531; his choir grille, 1518–1523.
tracks.listen: The friar who made the cathedral's ironwork, was paid in corn, and fixed the Giralda's clock.

tracks.title: Coro — The choir and the organs
tracks.where: At the crossing, now facing away from the altarpiece toward the Coro: a walled enclosure in the middle of the central nave, open only at its front, closed by a tall Renaissance iron grille, with organ pipes rising above the stalls [O8].
tracks.what: The Coro: Renaissance grille by Fray Francisco de Salamanca, 1518–1523; 117 carved seats in two tiers, Gothic-Mudéjar, misericords carved with the vices; King's chair signed by Nufro Sánchez, 1478, continued by Pieter Dancart from 1479; Renaissance lectern of wood and bronze, 1562–1565, bronze reliefs cast by Bartolomé Morel; the double organ, present organs finished 1903, electronic adaptation 1973; the left pillar of the choir collapsed in 1888 and was rebuilt.
tracks.listen: A carver's signature from 1478, the stalls and their hidden vices, the lectern by the Giraldillo's founder, and the twin organs.

tracks.title: Capilla de San Antonio — Murillo's Saint Anthony
tracks.where: In the side aisle on the side where you came down from the tower, toward the far end of the church, in front of the chapel grille of the Capilla de San Antonio, the baptistery chapel. Look for a huge canvas above the altar: a kneeling friar looking up at the Christ Child among a crowd of angels, with a smaller painting above it.
tracks.what: Bartolomé Esteban Murillo, Vision of Saint Anthony of Padua, set on this altar 21 Nov 1656, oil on canvas; above it Murillo's Baptism of Christ, 1667; the theft of the saint's figure, late 1874, recovered in New York, January 1875; stained-glass Santas Justa y Rufina by Juan Bautista de León, 1685, in this chapel.
tracks.listen: The night someone cut Saint Anthony out of Murillo's canvas, and how a New York dealer brought him home.

tracks.room: Puerta de la Asunción · west end, inside
tracks.title: West end — The oldest windows and the great doors
tracks.where: At the far end of the church from the Capilla Mayor, in front of the great central doors of the Puerta de la Asunción, seen from inside. Look up at the tall stained-glass window above the doors and along the windows of this half of the church.
tracks.what: Puerta de la Asunción, centre of the main front, completed 1827–1833 under Fernando Rosales, sculpture outside by Ricardo Bellver; the oldest stained glass, by Enrique Alemán, documented 1478–1483; the three windows of this front by Vicente Menardo, including the Evangelists above the main door.
tracks.listen: Why the cathedral's main doors waited centuries to be finished, and the oldest glass in the building.

tracks.title: Capilla de la Antigua — The Virgin who stayed
tracks.where: On the far side of the church from the tower, at the grille of the Capilla de la Antigua, the largest chapel on that side; its name is over the grille. Look for the medieval painted Virgin and Child above the altar.
tracks.what: Virgen de la Antigua, anonymous wall painting, 14th century, with Sienese influence; the chapel's enlargement begun 1504; tomb of Cardinal Diego Hurtado de Mendoza, placed 1510; canonical coronation 1929; San Fernando window designed by José Gestoso, made by Zettler of Munich.
tracks.listen: A painting older than the cathedral, the legend of the king who took Seville, and the Caribbean island named after her.

tracks.room: Sepulcro de Cristóbal Colón · south transept
tracks.title: Sepulcro de Colón — Four heralds
tracks.where: In the arm of the transept on the far side of the church from the tower, just inside the Puerta del Príncipe. Look for four figures of heralds carrying a coffin on their shoulders, raised high above the floor.
tracks.what: Arturo Mélida, monument to Christopher Columbus, designed for Havana Cathedral (competition 1891, installed there by March 1898), set up in Seville Cathedral 1902; the four heralds of Castile, León, Aragon and Navarre. The Puerta del Príncipe, also called the Puerta de San Cristóbal, by Adolfo Fernández Casanova in the Gothic style.
tracks.listen: A tomb built for Havana that ended up in Seville, and what its four heralds mean.

tracks.title: Sepulcro de Colón — Whose bones?
tracks.where: Still at the tomb of Columbus, by the Puerta del Príncipe: the coffin carried by four heralds.
tracks.what: The remains in Arturo Mélida's monument; their journey from Valladolid (1506) by way of the Cartuja in Seville, Santo Domingo and Havana; the 1877 Santo Domingo find; the University of Granada DNA studies announced in 2006 and 2024; Hernando Colón, buried in the cathedral, and his library.
tracks.listen: Columbus's long journey after death, two countries that claim his bones, and what the DNA studies can and cannot say.

tracks.title: Sacristía de los Cálices — Goya's potter saints
tracks.where: In the Sacristía de los Cálices, reached through the Capilla de los Dolores. Look for Goya's tall canvas, over three metres high: two young women saints holding pots, a lion at their feet, a broken statue on the ground and the Giralda behind them.
tracks.what: Francisco de Goya, Santas Justa y Rufina, 1817, oil on canvas, 309 × 177 cm, commissioned by the cathedral chapter through Juan Agustín Ceán Bermúdez, delivered 14 January 1818.
tracks.listen: How Goya painted Seville's two potter saints for the cathedral, the tower they are said to have saved, and why local painters were furious.

tracks.title: Sala del Pabellón · Extra · Zurbarán and Seville's painters
tracks.where: In the Sala del Pabellón, the exhibition room of the sacristies. Look for the labels naming Zurbarán, Valdés Leal and Pacheco.
tracks.what: Francisco de Zurbarán, two paintings, 1635–1645 and 1645–1650; Juan de Valdés Leal, two paintings, around 1656 and 1657–1658; Francisco Pacheco, 1620. All five placed in this room by the Cathedral's own list, which gives no titles. El Greco loan held until O13/O22, see v5/notes/AUDIT_FIXES_001-028.md.
tracks.listen: Two Zurbaráns where the Cathedral's own list places them, beside Valdés Leal and the teacher of Velázquez.

tracks.title: Sacristía Mayor — Campaña's Descent
tracks.where: In the Sacristía Mayor, the great domed sacristy. Stand facing the central chapel: in front of it hangs Pedro de Campaña's large painting of Christ's body being lowered from the cross.
tracks.what: Pedro de Campaña, Descent from the Cross, 1547, painted for the chapel of Hernando de Jaén in the parish church of Santa Cruz, Seville.
tracks.listen: The painting Murillo could not stop looking at, and the church that both of them lost.

tracks.title: Sacristía Mayor · Extra · A dome of the Last Judgment
tracks.where: In the middle of the Sacristía Mayor, under the dome. Look up at the dome carved in three rings of figures; then find Murillo's two paintings of San Isidoro and San Leandro, and, at the head of the room, the statue of San Fernando beside one pillar and the Immaculate Conception on the pillar opposite.
tracks.what: The Sacristía Mayor, a Greek-cross plan with very short arms and a dome on pendentives, its reliefs showing the Last Judgment and the Heavenly Court in three rings; Bartolomé Esteban Murillo, San Isidoro and San Leandro, 1655; statue of San Fernando made for his canonisation of 1671, next to one of the pillars at the head, and an Immaculate Conception on the opposite pillar.
tracks.listen: Reading a dome of the Last Judgment from the bottom ring up, and Murillo's two archbishops of Seville.

tracks.title: Sacristía Mayor — The Custodia de Arfe
tracks.where: In the Sacristía Mayor, in front of the Custodia de Arfe: a tall silver monstrance, taller than a person, built up in storeys of columns that narrow toward the top.
tracks.what: Juan de Arfe y Villafañe, the great processional monstrance (Custodia grande), silver, model accepted 1580, completed 1587; part of a collection of about nine hundred pieces of gold and silverware.
tracks.listen: The silver tower that still goes out into the streets of Seville every Corpus Christi, and the goldsmith who designed it.

tracks.title: Sala Capitular · Extra · An oval for the chapter
tracks.where: Inside the Sala Capitular, reached from the Antecabildo through a curved corridor: an oval room with carved reliefs and paintings of the Virtues around the walls and a ring of round paintings high in the vault. Stand to one side, out of the doorway.
tracks.what: The chapter house: elliptical plan, begun in the mid-16th century under Hernán Ruiz II, completed by Asensio de Maeda; programme with Latin inscriptions by Canon Francisco Pacheco; Pablo de Céspedes, the Virtues, 1592; large reliefs by Juan Bautista Vázquez el Viejo and Diego de Velasco, c. 1582; rectangular reliefs by Marcos Cabrera, c. 1590; Diego de Velasco, carved mahogany armchair, 1592.
tracks.listen: Why the canons' meeting room is an oval, and the moral lesson carved and painted round its walls.

tracks.title: Sala Capitular — Murillo's Immaculate
tracks.where: In the Sala Capitular, the oval chapter house. Look up into the vault: a ring of eight round paintings of saints, and above them, in a carved frame, the large painting of the Virgin.
tracks.what: Bartolomé Esteban Murillo, Immaculate Conception, commissioned 1667, painted 1667–68, in a carved frame, with eight Sevillian saints on round canvases around the vault. Also named: Murillo's San Isidoro and San Leandro, 1655 (Sacristía Mayor); Vision of St Anthony (Capilla de San Antonio); works in the Capilla de Santiago (1674) and at the Ángel de la Guarda altar (1665–66); Pedro de Campaña, Descent from the Cross, 1547 (Sacristía Mayor).
tracks.listen: The painter whose work runs all through this cathedral, and the Virgin he set above the canons' heads.

tracks.section: Royal chapel and the way to the courtyard
tracks.title: Capilla Real — The king who took Seville
tracks.where: Outside the great iron grille of the Capilla Real, at the end of the church behind the Capilla Mayor. Stand back from the grille, to one side, so that people at prayer and other visitors can pass; a sculpture of the saint-king receiving the keys of Seville crowns the grille.
tracks.what: Capilla Real (Royal Chapel): designed and directed by Martín de Gainza from 1551, dome completed about 1568 by Hernán Ruiz II, lantern rebuilt after a 1754 collapse; Virgen de los Reyes, 13th-century Gothic image "of French origin", under a silver canopy; tombs of Alfonso X and Beatriz of Swabia in the side walls; crypt with Pedro I and María de Padilla (not visible); urn of San Fernando by the silversmith Juan Laureano de Pina, made after the 1671 canonisation; entrance grille designed by Sebastián van der Borcht, paid for by Charles III, installed 1771, crowned by Jerónimo Roldán's San Fernando receiving the keys of Seville. Worship only (NORMAS).
tracks.listen: The king who turned the mosque into a cathedral, the family that lies with him, and why we look from the grille.

tracks.section: Royal chapel and the way to the courtyard
tracks.room: Puerta de la Concepción · north transept
tracks.title: Puerta de la Concepción — Back to the mosque's courtyard
tracks.where: Inside the church, at the end wall of the arm of the transept on the tower's side, facing the Puerta de la Concepción: the tall Gothic doorway at the end of this arm of the transept. Stand back from the door, out of the flow of people going through.
tracks.what: Puerta de la Concepción, on the north front of the transept, opening onto the Patio de los Naranjos; completed in Gothic style by Adolfo Fernández Casanova (date not spoken: 1887 on the building page, 1917 on the timeline). Above it, Arnao de Flandes, The Ascension, stained glass, 1539–1541; Arnao also made thirteen windows of saints in the transept.
tracks.listen: A door that looks medieval but was finished in modern times, the Ascension window above it, and the courtyard of the mosque beyond.

tracks.title: Patio de los Naranjos — The mosque's courtyard
tracks.where: In the Patio de los Naranjos, the large open courtyard beside the cathedral: rows of orange trees in a grid, small water channels between them, a fountain in the middle, and arcades of pointed horseshoe arches along the sides, with the Giralda rising above. Stand under the trees or by an arcade, out of the path to the exit.
tracks.what: The former sahn (ablutions courtyard) of the Almohad Great Mosque, ordered 1172: original pillars and pointed horseshoe arches; of three galleries two remain, the third demolished for the Sagrario church (1618–1662); orange trees in a rigid grid with water channels still in use; modern fountain on the site of the old sabil, its upper bowl Visigothic and "the same as the primitive Almohad fountain" (Cathedral).
tracks.listen: How the mosque's washing courtyard survived the mosque, and the oldest thing in it.

tracks.room: Patio de los Naranjos · view of the Giralda
tracks.title: Patio de los Naranjos — The Giraldillo
tracks.where: In the Patio de los Naranjos, at a spot under the orange trees where you can see the very top of the Giralda: a bronze female figure holding a banner, standing on the highest point of the belfry.
tracks.what: The Giraldillo, "Faith Victorious", bronze, about 4 m high and about 1,500 kg, a turning weathervane figure holding a palm and a banner (labarum); cast by Bartolomé Morel (contract 27 Aug 1566), designed by the painter Luis de Vargas (AHPS; IAPH: "no conclusive documents"); placed on the tower 13 Aug 1568; probably based on a print of Pallas Athena; taken down for study in Dec 1998, the original put back 22 July 2005.
tracks.listen: The bronze figure that gave the Giralda its name, the goddess she may have started as, and why the one on top is the original.

tracks.title: Nave del Lagarto — A crocodile, a tusk and a giraffe
tracks.where: In the Nave del Lagarto, the covered gallery along the side of the Patio de los Naranjos nearest the Giralda. Look up at the ceiling for a crocodile hanging overhead, with an elephant tusk, a rod and a bridle near it.
tracks.what: Hanging objects: a crocodile (the "lagarto"), said to be a carved wooden copy today; an elephant tusk; a rod of command; a bridle. The embassy of the Mamluk Sultan of Egypt to Alfonso X, c. 1260 (between 1260 and 1265), with "un marfil", a giraffe ("azorafa") and a striped she-ass (zebra) in the Crónica de Alfonso X; the crocodile added by tradition and by Ortiz de Zúñiga (17th c.). Above the gallery: the Biblioteca Capitular y Colombina (not on the visit).
tracks.listen: The true story of a sultan's gifts to a Spanish king, the crocodile that tradition added to them, and what really hangs here now.

tracks.title: Puerta del Perdón — The way out
tracks.where: At the Puerta del Perdón, the tall arched gateway in the middle of the side of the Patio de los Naranjos opposite the cathedral, the way out. Stand to one side of the arch, out of the flow of people leaving, before you go through.
tracks.what: Puerta del Perdón: original Almohad gate, the main entrance to the mosque's courtyard, aligned with the mosque's central nave and mihrab; carved plaster inside the arch; front renovated 1520 with terracottas by Miguel Florentín (St Peter and St Paul at the sides, the Virgin and the Archangel Gabriel above them); Plateresque plasterwork by Bartolomé López, 1522; relief of the Expulsion of the Merchants just above the arch (which face: O18). Recorded in 3D by the Factum Foundation with the Cabildo, Nov 2025. The roofs: a separate visit.
tracks.listen: The mosque's own front gate, the Christian figures added to it, and the three buildings you have walked through in one.
